sections.final_normalized_text: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples2. Subject-Specific Content & Key ExamplesListen for the ideaAfter a short spoken message, restate the key point before adding a response.Build on another speakerUse a response such as “I agree with ___ because…” or “I see it differently because…” and connect directly to what was said.Voice supports purposePractise pace, volume and emphasis on the same sentence, then discuss which delivery best suits the audience and purpose.Use source-based cultural evidenceWhen a text, language name or cultural protocol is discussed, identify the source and describe what it supports without treating one example as representing all First Nations Peoples or Countries/Places.A complete message to hear and restateAdult or partner models this whole message in the learner’s communication mode: “Our paper bridge needs a wide base. That will help it stand. Then we can add the road.” A possible restatement is “The wide base comes first so the bridge can stand.” A connected addition is “Could we add supports beside the base?” Rephrase rather than demand exact repetition.One sentence in two occasionsSentence: “Could we compare the two designs?” Occasion A: two familiar partners are choosing a bridge. Occasion B: a chaired school meeting; the chair invites a student question. Model the same clear sentence in both contexts, attending to the agreed turn. Discuss how the wording can suit both and how the occasion changes when a turn is taken. Pace and comfortable volume support communication; they are not separate performance targets here.Source-backed roles and checked host guidanceReconciliation Australia explains that a Welcome to Country is delivered by Traditional Owners, or Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander people given permission by Traditional Owners. Anyone can offer an Acknowledgement of Country. The roles and purposes differ; arrangements and appropriate wording depend on context. Consult local representative bodies and the actual hosts when planning an event.For a real visit, ask the host how to participate and when to ask questions. The fictional host directions used in this lesson are supplied for that scenario only. Do not turn them into rules for every First Nations community, invent local language or imitate a ceremony.Read Reconciliation Australia’s explanation of Welcome and Acknowledgement rolesDisplay discussion · another roundThe group has three paper models: a boat, a bridge and a bird. Proposed plan: all models go on a low table; labels go beside their objects; a wide gap stays clear for visitors. Eva says, “Let’s put the bridge in the middle so people can see both sides.”Restate Eva’s idea, add a connected suggestion, ask a useful question and negotiate moving on to the display title.For example: “You want the bridge in the middle so both sides can be seen. Could the boat go at one end? How much space should we leave? When we have agreed on places, could we choose the title?” Accept equivalent relevant language and a real chance for others to reply. Check the group’s final plan by asking what each person will do.

Outcome Overview & Core ConceptsStudents learn to understand how the language of evaluation and emotion, such as modal verbs, can be varied to be more or less forceful. They identify the relevant language or text feature, point to evidence and explain how it contributes to meaning or purpose. Key concepts include language, vocabulary, character.

sections.label: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples
sections.final_normalized_text: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples2. Subject-Specific Content & Key ExamplesOpinion plus reasonMove from “I liked the story” to “I found the ending effective because the repeated warning built suspense.” The second response gives a judgement and evidence.Strength of judgementIn a prediction about a new lid, compare “The lid might help keep the paint wet” with “The lid will help keep the paint wet”: the second sounds more certain. In a recommendation, “You should put the lid on” advises an action. A recommendation and a prediction do different jobs; do not rank their modals on one universal ladder.Subjective and objective wording“The brilliant new playground is exciting” evaluates; “the playground opened on Monday” reports a checkable fact. Discuss why a writer may choose either.TransferUse the complete revision cards below. Identify the word choice, change it for the stated context and explain the changed force, attitude or emotion.The complete warning story behind the opinion“Keep the lid shut or the paper stars will blow away,” said the keeper. Dara nodded and put the lid down. A gust shook the table. “Keep the lid shut,” the keeper warned again. Dara reached for the ribbon, the lid lifted, and the stars scattered across the floor. Dara and the keeper gathered every star and tied the lid down.A reader can support “I found the ending effective because the repeated warning built suspense” by naming the repeated warning and the later scattering. That is one supported judgement, not a response everyone must share.A complete record and a judgementPrepared fictional record: “The new playground opened on Monday. It has two swings.” Response: “The brilliant new playground is exciting.” The record supplies checkable model facts; brilliant and exciting add evaluation or feeling. Explain whose judgement is being expressed rather than claiming every reader must feel excited.Revision card 1 · an offered choiceA group leader wants to offer drawing as one possible quiet activity. The draft says, “You must draw while we wait.”Replace the modal so it offers the activity as a choice, and explain the effect.“You could draw while we wait” offers a possibility or suggestion instead of a requirement. Other clear choice wording, such as “You can choose to draw”, can work; explain how it fits the stated purpose.Revision card 2 · a narrator’s impressionVersion A: “The rabbit pushed past the other animals.” Version B: “The rabbit politely waited for the other animals.” These fictional versions deliberately give different actions and attitudes.Name a verb and an adverb that create the different evaluations. Does changing A into B preserve all facts?Pushed contrasts with waited, and politely presents an approving attitude in B. The action has changed as well as the impression, so the versions do not preserve all facts. A writer may choose either for a different fictional character portrayal.Revision card 3 · stronger pleasure“At last, the repaired kite flew. Sol felt pleased with the result.” The writer wants stronger pleasure, not anger or fear.Replace pleased and explain why your word fits the intended feeling.Delighted is one suitable choice: it expresses stronger pleasure in this context. Thrilled may also work. Terrified would change the emotion to fear, and furious would change it to anger.

sections.final_normalized_text: Practice Thought & Formative AssessmentPractice Thought & Formative AssessmentUse a fresh example that has not been modelled. Ask the student to show the exact clue, feature or language choice and explain or use it independently.Fresh check · probability and obligationA rule says, “Visitors must stay behind the line.” A prediction says, “The bus could arrive early.”Explain the modal’s job in each sentence. Rewrite the prediction to sound more certain without turning it into a rule.Must expresses a requirement to stay behind the line. Could expresses a possible arrival. “The bus will arrive early” sounds more certain as a prediction; it is still the speaker’s claim rather than proof of the future.Fresh check · noun, verb and adverb choicesFictional narrator A: “The helper gently guided the lost cub.” Narrator B: “The troublemaker roughly shoved the lost cub.”Compare one noun, one verb and one adverb and explain the impressions. Are these merely different spellings of the same facts?Helper/troublemaker gives approving/disapproving labels; guided/shoved changes the action and force; gently/roughly changes manner. The versions present meaningfully different behaviour and evaluations, so they are not fact-preserving swaps. Discuss fictional actions rather than fixed labels for classmates.Fresh check · supported judgement“Uma saw that the display sign had fallen. She set it upright so visitors could read it. Then she returned to her own work.”Give a supported judgement of Uma’s action and a reason. Then express mild or strong pleasure in your own response and name which you chose.Helpful or thoughtful is supported by setting the sign upright for visitors. For example, “I was pleased that Uma helped” expresses pleasure; “I was delighted that Uma helped” expresses stronger pleasure in this comparison. Accept another accurate judgement or response with evidence; do not infer an exact hidden feeling for Uma.

sections.label: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples
sections.final_normalized_text: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples2. Subject-Specific Content & Key ExamplesStructure follows purposeA procedure uses ordered steps because sequence matters; a story may organise events to build tension; an information report groups related facts under headings.Cohesion across sentencesCompare “Mia found a shell. Mia washed the shell.” with “Mia found a shell. She washed it.” The pronoun connects ideas without unnecessary repetition.Paragraph focusA paragraph is easier to follow when its sentences develop one main idea rather than jumping between unrelated points.TransferUse the complete mixed-up text below. Make a useful organisation or connection change, then explain exactly how it helps the reader.Complete extra structure modelsProcedure, “Make a paper name card”: “Materials: a sheet of paper and a pencil. First, fold the paper in half. Next, write the model’s name on the front. Finally, stand the folded card beside the model.” The sequence tells the reader what to do.Information report, “Our name cards”: “Materials: Each card is paper. Shape: Each folded card stands like a small tent. Use: A card names the model beside it.” Grouped facts help the reader find materials, shape or use.Narrative, “The missing card”: “Jo placed a card beside the model boat. A breeze blew the card under the table. Jo found it and put a small weight on it. The visitors could read the boat’s name.” The linked events introduce and resolve a problem.Complete mixed-up recount for the retained transfer taskSentence cards: A “Finally, we put the labelled models on the table.” B “On Thursday, our class prepared a display.” C “First, we made the models; then we wrote their labels.”Arrange the three cards into a clear recount and explain one organising change.B, C, A gives the occasion before the ordered events and ending. The time words and the need to make and label models before displaying them support that order. The repair helps a reader follow what happened; it is more than changing a pronoun.

sections.final_normalized_text: Practice Thought & Formative AssessmentPractice Thought & Formative AssessmentUse a fresh example that has not been modelled. Ask the student to show the exact clue, feature or language choice and explain or use it independently.Fresh comparison · recount and autobiographical modelClass reporter’s factual recount: “On Monday, our class measured the display tables. First, the teacher gave each group a ruler. Next, the groups recorded the lengths. Finally, the class compared the records.” Fictional autobiographical model written in invented character Dev’s voice: “I first enjoyed measuring when I helped make a toy house. I measured its walls with my aunt. Later, I started keeping drawings of my designs. I still like finding out how things fit.”Compare purpose, viewpoint and one organising choice in the two complete texts.The factual recount records a particular class event in time order, using first/next/finally. Dev’s model selects experiences from the character’s own life in I/my voice and ends with a personal reflection. Both use past experiences. The autobiographical model is explicitly fictional; I alone is not proof that a text is a true autobiography.Fresh comparison · report and explanationReport, “Our balancing model”: “Parts: A card strip rests on a block. A small toy sits on each end. Position: The block is under the middle of the strip.” Explanation, “How this model tips”: “At first, the strip rests level on the block. When we move one toy farther from the middle, that end of this prepared model goes down. The changed toy position makes this model tip.”Which text groups parts and position, and which follows a change and its result? Explain how the arrangement serves each purpose.The report groups facts under Parts and Position so a reader can find a property of the model. The explanation connects the changed position to the observed tipping result in this prepared model. It explains how the change occurs rather than listing parts. No calculation or general physics rule is required.Fresh comparison · story, verse and responseNarrative, “The loose wheel”: “In art time, Lin’s paper cart lost a wheel. Lin could not make it stand. Ari held the cart while Lin fixed the wheel. The cart rolled across the desk, and both children cheered.” Verse, “Paper cart”: “Wobble, little paper wheel; / wait beside the line. / Steady hands can help you stand; / now your turn to shine.” Personal response: “I liked The loose wheel because Ari’s small act of holding the cart makes the repair possible.”Describe one organisation or language choice in each text and connect it to its purpose.The story links a problem, help and resolution to entertain through events. The verse uses four lines, repeated sounds or imagined address to a wheel, creating a playful focus rather than merely listing facts. The response gives a view and a story-based reason. Accept other accurate feature-effect links; do not require everyone to like the story.Fresh comparison · argument and informationArgument: “We should keep a ruler beside the display table. First, makers could check whether a model fits the space. Second, visitors could measure a model if the teacher invites them to. Let’s keep one ruler in a labelled place.” Information: “The class ruler is 30 centimetres long. It is kept beside the display table. Its marks show centimetres.”Identify the four argument stages and compare the main purposes of the texts. Why would “The ruler is yellow” be a weak extra reason for this proposal?The argument introduces a proposal, gives a fit-checking reason, gives a visitor-measuring reason, and concludes with an action request. It aims to persuade; the other text informs about the ruler. Colour is merely related information unless a further relevant reason is explained. It does not by itself support keeping a ruler there.

sections.label: Learning goals
sections.final_normalized_text: Learning goals1. Outcome Overview & Core ConceptsStudents learn to understand that a clause is a unit of grammar usually containing a subject and a verb that need to agree. They identify the relevant language or text feature, point to evidence and explain how it contributes to meaning or purpose. Key concepts include clause.

sections.label: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples
sections.final_normalized_text: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples2. Subject-Specific Content & Key ExamplesBuild the sentenceStart with “Birds fly.” Add precise information: “Small shorebirds fly quickly across the inlet.” Identify what each added word or group contributes.Clause relationshipCompare “We stayed inside because it rained” with “It rained, so we stayed inside.” Both connect ideas, but the clause structure foregrounds the relationship differently.Grammar changes meaningCompare “The dog chased the ball” with “The ball was chased by the dog.” The event is similar, but the sentence foregrounds different information.TransferStudents change one grammatical feature in a new sentence, then explain what changed in meaning, emphasis, time or detail.Complete clause cardsThe small rabbit is quiet.The rabbits beside the pond are quiet.The basket of leaves rest by the door.Mina and Jo carries the basket.While the wind blew, the children were reading indoors.Mark each whole subject and verb group. Repair cards 3 and 4. Then join “The dog slept” and “The children painted” with while. Say which clause needs the rest of the resulting sentence.Check and explain1: The small rabbit / is. 2: The rabbits beside the pond / are. 3: The basket of leaves / rests. 4: Mina and Jo / carry. 5: the wind / blew; the children / were reading. One joined version is “While the dog slept, the children painted.” The while part depends on its partner here. A valid alternative is “The dog slept while the children painted”; identify the while clause in the actual version.Answers for the earlier grammar comparisonsIn “Small shorebirds fly quickly across the inlet”, small describes the shorebirds, quickly describes their manner of flying, and across the inlet adds location. The whole subject is Small shorebirds; fly is the verb. “We stayed inside because it rained” contains we / stayed and it / rained. The because part gives the reason. “It rained, so we stayed inside” presents the rain first and makes the result explicit. Formal clause labels are not required.In “The dog chased the ball”, the dog is the subject and chased is the verb. In “The ball was chased by the dog”, the ball is the subject and was chased is the whole verb group. The subject is not always the doer. These forms retain the same chasing event; this is a supported comparison, not a requirement to master passive forms.Fresh transfer: change “The dog near the trees runs” so it names two dogs. One answer is “The dogs near the trees run”. Changing the subject number requires changing this present verb too.

Pointing only to pens misses the main subject word. In “The box is full”, is is already a verb. A correct explanation names the subject and the matching form.

sections.final_normalized_text: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples2. Subject-Specific Content & Key ExamplesDoing and saying in a complete sceneRead: “Jo opened the gate. ‘Come in,’ Jo whispered.” Opened tells what Jo did to the gate; whispered tells how Jo spoke the invitation. Compare “Jo shouted, ‘Come in.’” Shouted is also a saying verb, but suggests louder delivery. The verb does not tell us why Jo spoke loudly.Thinking and feelingRead: “Jo remembered the ending. Jo liked the story.” Remembered gives a thinking meaning: Jo recalls something. Liked gives a feeling meaning: Jo has a positive response to the story. Compare “Jo loved the story.” Loved usually expresses a stronger positive feeling here; liked and loved both tell feeling. No knowledge of the story’s events is needed to explain these verbs.Relating a subject to a description or featureRead these complete sentences: “The brilliant new playground is exciting.” “The playground opened on Monday.” “It has two slides.” Is relates the playground to a description. Has relates it to a feature it possesses. Opened tells an event. Brilliant and exciting contribute descriptions, but is is the relating verb in the first sentence. Explain what each verb tells us in its clause.Read the whole verb group in contextCompare “The gardener is quiet” and “The gardener is digging beside the fence”. Find the relating verb in the first clause and the whole doing verb group in the second. Check: is relates the gardener to a description in the first clause; is digging is the whole group describing an action in the second. Is helps digging there. The meaning depends on the complete clause, not is alone.A complete story with all five verb meanings“Fen opened the box. ‘Here it is,’ Fen said. Fen remembered the missing key and loved its shiny ribbon. The key had a round handle.”Find opened, said, remembered, loved and had. Explain the different information each gives. Is in the quoted speech also relates it to here in this context.Check and explainOpened: doing, an action with the box. Said: saying, a spoken message. Remembered: thinking, a memory. Loved: feeling about its ribbon. Had: relating, a feature possessed by the key. These are different kinds of meaning in these exact clauses.Use the earlier evaluation examples to inspect verbsThe earlier examples also contain verbs. In “I liked the story”, liked expresses a feeling. In “The playground opened on Monday”, opened presents an event. In “The playground is exciting”, is relates the playground to a description. The words brilliant and exciting evaluate the playground but are not whole verb groups in that description.Complete fresh comparison: “Jo whispered, ‘The gate is open.’” Change whispered to shouted. Both are saying verbs. Shouted changes the indicated delivery; it does not establish Jo’s reason or feeling. For the earlier stronger/weaker judgement task, compare “I liked the ending” and “I loved the ending”. Both express a positive feeling, with loved usually stronger in this context. Accept a supported explanation of a different intended feeling.

sections.label: Common Student Misconceptions
sections.final_normalized_text: Common Student Misconceptions3. Common Student MisconceptionsFeature spotting: Explain how the exact feature shapes meaning, communication or response.Retelling: Select precise evidence and analyse it rather than repeating content.Automatic effect: Interpret choices through audience, purpose, context and surrounding text.Vague explanation: Replace “this makes it better” with the exact feature, evidence and likely effect.A concrete quick correctionIn “Fen remembered the key”, remembered is a verb even though it does not name visible movement. In “The key has a round handle”, has relates a feature to the key. Naming the verb is a start; explain the particular information it gives.

Ask the student to show the exact clue, feature or language choice and explain or use it independently.A fresh five-meaning check“Sam carried the tray. ‘It is heavy,’ Sam said. Sam remembered the spilled water and disliked the slippery floor. The tray had two handles.” Find a verb for doing, saying, thinking, feeling and relating. Explain the information each gives.Check and explainCarried: doing, the movement of the tray. Said: saying, the spoken comment. Remembered: thinking, a memory. Disliked: feeling about the floor. Had: relating, possession of handles. Is also relates it to heavy. Accept either clear relating example. Use meanings in the actual clauses.

sections.label: Learning goals
sections.final_normalized_text: Learning goals1. Outcome Overview & Core ConceptsStudents learn to understand that verbs are anchored in time through tense. They identify the relevant language or text feature, point to evidence and explain how it contributes to meaning or purpose. Key concepts include meaning, language choices, audience.

sections.label: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples
sections.final_normalized_text: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples2. Subject-Specific Content & Key ExamplesBuild the sentenceStart with “Birds fly.” Add precise information: “Small shorebirds fly quickly across the inlet.” Identify what each added word or group contributes.Clause relationshipCompare “We stayed inside because it rained” with “It rained, so we stayed inside.” Both connect ideas, but the clause structure foregrounds the relationship differently.Grammar changes meaningCompare “The dog chased the ball” with “The ball was chased by the dog.” The event is similar, but the sentence foregrounds different information.TransferStudents change one grammatical feature in a new sentence, then explain what changed in meaning, emphasis, time or detail.Complete time cardsHabit: Each morning Jo ___ the plants. Use water.Completed yesterday: Jo ___ the plants and ___ home. Use water and go.Plan for tomorrow: Jo will ___ the plants. Use water.Recount to repair: Yesterday we made a sign. We put it by the bed and carry the tools home.Choose the forms and explain the time. Finally write a new garden message with one past event, one present habit and one future plan.Check and explain1: waters, a present habit. 2: watered and went, past events. 3: water, the base form after will. 4: change carry to carried. Made and put already fit the past recount. An original message might be “Yesterday we planted beans. We water them each morning. Tomorrow we will check the soil.” Accept other clear messages with matching forms and explicit intended time changes.Apply time changes to the earlier examples“Small shorebirds fly quickly across the inlet” uses fly; to describe one completed event yesterday, write “Small shorebirds flew quickly across the inlet yesterday”. Flew is the past form of fly. The added describing words do not create the tense change.“We stayed inside because it rained” and “It rained, so we stayed inside” both use past verbs, stayed and rained. Their different ordering shows the reason/result relationship, not a change in time. “The dog chased the ball” and “The ball was chased by the dog” both describe the past chasing event. Was chased is the whole group in the second form; formal passive terminology is not required.Fresh transfer: change “The children carry the box” into a completed event yesterday and a plan for tomorrow. Answers: “Yesterday the children carried the box” and “Tomorrow the children will carry the box”. Explain carried and will carry.

sections.label: Common Student Misconceptions
sections.final_normalized_text: Common Student Misconceptions3. Common Student MisconceptionsFeature spotting: Explain how the exact feature shapes meaning, communication or response.Retelling: Select precise evidence and analyse it rather than repeating content.Automatic effect: Interpret choices through audience, purpose, context and surrounding text.Vague explanation: Replace “this makes it better” with the exact feature, evidence and likely effect.A concrete quick correctionIn “Yesterday Jo took a cup”, took supplies past form and yesterday makes the time explicit. Do not replace took with taked. An explanation should name both the form and intended time rather than saying it sounds better.

sections.label: Practice Thought & Formative Assessment
sections.final_normalized_text: Practice Thought & Formative AssessmentPractice Thought & Formative AssessmentUse a fresh example that has not been modelled. Ask the student to show the exact clue, feature or language choice and explain or use it independently.A fresh time checkThis message has two yesterday events and one tomorrow plan: “Yesterday Jo caught a ball. Jo carry it home. Tomorrow Jo will play again.” Repair the middle verb, identify the whole future group and explain why one time change stays.Check and explainUse carried. Caught and carried describe yesterday’s events; will play is the whole future group. The tomorrow plan is a justified change of time. “Will plays” would not fit this construction.

sections.label: Learning goals
sections.final_normalized_text: Learning goals1. Outcome Overview & Core ConceptsStudents learn to identify how images extend the meaning of a text. They identify the relevant language or text feature, point to evidence and explain how it contributes to meaning or purpose. Key concepts include image, character.

sections.label: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples
sections.final_normalized_text: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples2. Subject-Specific Content & Key ExamplesWords and image togetherA caption may name what a photograph shows while the image supplies colour, scale or expression that the words do not. Explain the contribution of each mode.Framing directs attentionA close-up makes a face or object prominent; a wide view can emphasise setting and distance. Ask what the viewer is guided to notice.Layout supports navigationHeadings, labels, diagrams and white space can help readers locate and connect information rather than merely decorate the page.TransferShow a new still or multimodal text. Students identify one visual choice and explain how it adds, extends or changes the written meaning.Actual images for the earlier visual tasksJo met Kim.JoKimJo met Kim. Jo and Kim are similar in depicted size, stand close, face each other and smile. Their hands reach towards the same box.Ari waited.Close viewWide viewBoth panels say Ari waited. In the close view Ari’s large face looks towards the viewer with both pupils forward. In the wide view a small Ari faces away across a large empty space.The meeting drawing adds facing direction, distance, expression and a shared object. The viewer comparison changes framing and gaze while keeping its words the same. These are drawings, not photographs. For the earlier transfer task, use the different gate try below rather than an unseen picture.Try: The two people waited.gateGate try: The two people waited. Two similar-sized figures stand far apart. The left figure faces left and the right figure faces right. Both have folded arms and straight mouths.Check and explainThe gate try shows widely spaced figures facing away, folded arms and straight mouths. These details may suggest distance or disagreement. The written caption alone supplies only waiting. The reason and earlier events remain unknown.A useful labelled diagramUse the preserved picnic-area map in Worked example and reasoning checks. The labels identify the picnic area, creek and bridge; the dotted line shows a walking route to the bridge. That image supplies route information beyond “The picnic area is beside the creek”. Layout can help us locate a label; the route itself supplies the added meaning.

sections.label: Common Student Misconceptions
sections.final_normalized_text: Common Student Misconceptions3. Common Student MisconceptionsFeature spotting: Naming a camera angle, colour or sound is not analysis; explain its effect.One fixed effect: Interpret the feature in context and alongside other modes.Separate-mode lists: Explain how image, words and sound reinforce, contradict or qualify one another.Retelling: Analyse how the representation was constructed, not only what it shows.A concrete quick correctionIn the meeting drawing, the shared box and facing figures may suggest cooperation. “They have been best friends for years” goes beyond the evidence. A close face may invite attention, but viewers do not all have to feel the same emotion.

sections.label: Practice Thought & Formative Assessment
sections.final_normalized_text: Practice Thought & Formative AssessmentPractice Thought & Formative AssessmentUse a fresh example that has not been modelled. Ask the student to show the exact clue, feature or language choice and explain or use it independently.A fresh visual version to createUse this new caption: “The friends found the box.” Draw two figures far apart, one facing the other and offering the box. Add a second version with the figures close together, both reaching for it. Explain a visible difference and a possible difference in relationship. Name something the words and images leave unknown.Check and explainCheck the actual drawing: the caption stays the same and the specified position or gesture changes are visible. For example, an offered box may suggest an invitation, while both reaching could suggest sharing or competing, depending on the drawn expressions. Accept supported possibilities; the drawings do not prove ownership or earlier events.

sections.label: Worked example and reasoning checks
sections.final_normalized_text: Worked example and reasoning checks Notice information supplied by an imageExplain how an image adds meaning beyond the accompanying words.Worked exampleThe words say ‘The picnic area is beside the creek.’ A map also marks a bridge upstream and a walking route to that bridge. What does the map add?Picnic area and bridgeA creek runs from the top to the bottom of the map. A picnic area is on its left bank. A dotted walking route leads upstream from the picnic area to a bridge crossing the creek.Picnic areaBridgeCreekWater flows downDotted line: walking routeThe words locate the picnic area. The map adds a route to a crossing.First identify the written information: the picnic area's position beside the creek.Read the map's symbols and route. They provide extra information about how to reach the other side.Explain the added meaning: the map shows where to cross at a bridge, which the sentence does not tell us.Watch for this mistake: Saying ‘the picture makes it interesting’ does not explain added meaning. Name a particular visible detail and the information it gives.Try it, then explainA story says ‘We finally arrived.’ Use the arrival illustration supplied below. Name information added by the image.HintUse specific details visible in the arrival illustration, rather than guessing a whole backstory.Answer and explanationThe children are muddy and the map is torn; these details suggest a difficult journey, although its exact events are not certain.Why is ‘The map shows a bridge upstream’ stronger evidence than ‘The map is nice’?HintChoose the comment that names visible information.Answer and explanationIt identifies a specific feature and location the reader can use. The actual arrival illustration for the earlier tryWe finally arrived.mapWe finally arrived. Two children have brown mud patches on their clothes and legs. Between them they hold a paper map with a jagged tear through its middle. The picture does not show how the mud or tear happened.

sections.label: Learning goals
sections.final_normalized_text: Learning goals1. Outcome Overview & Core ConceptsStudents learn to extend topic-specific and technical vocabulary and know that words can have different meanings in different contexts. They identify the relevant language or text feature, point to evidence and explain how it contributes to meaning or purpose. Key concepts include context, vocabulary, character, setting, plot.

sections.label: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples
sections.final_normalized_text: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples2. Subject-Specific Content & Key ExamplesMeaning from word partsIn “unhelpful”, identify un- + help + -ful. Use the base and affixes to predict meaning, then check it in the sentence.Spelling familyConnect related words such as help, helpful and helpless. The stable base helps students read, spell and understand the family.Choose by meaning in contextUse a word’s meaningful parts as clues, then read the whole sentence and check its meaning. “The helpful note showed us the way” uses helpful for something that helps. This lesson practises meaning and use; a separate spelling lesson can examine spelling choices.TransferUse “Jo reread the helpful note”. Students identify re- + read and help + -ful, explain read again and a note that helps, then use one related word in a new sentence.Complete vocabulary cardsMeasurement record: a card is 9 centimetres long and 4 centimetres wide; its edge strip is 3 millimetres wide. Report the card’s length and the strip’s width using number and unit.Story: “At noon beside the pond, a duck named Dot lost a feather. A frog found it and Dot put it in a nest.” Use character, setting and plot to describe this story.Two senses: “The feather is light. It weighs almost nothing.” “We need light to see the nest.” Explain light in each sentence, using a nearby clue.Word family: “The first drawing was unclear. I will draw it again.” Replace draw it again with redraw it. Explain re-. Then use help + -ful in a sentence about a clue that helps.Check and explain1: The card is 9 centimetres long; the strip is 3 millimetres wide. 2: Dot and the frog are characters; noon beside the pond gives the setting; losing, finding and placing the feather are plot events. 3: Light feather means not heavy; light to see means illumination. Weighs almost nothing and see help choose. 4: Re- means again in redraw. For example, “The helpful clue showed us where to look.” Helpful describes something that helps.Check the earlier word-family examples“The helpful note showed us the way” means the note helped. “The unhelpful note sent us to the wrong place” means it did not help. “Without a map, the lost toy felt helpless” means unable to help itself in this story. Help is the shared base; -ful, un- and -less change the meaning.Try a different related word: “The room was tidy. After the game it was ___.” Use un- + tidy. Answer: untidy, meaning not tidy. Check it in the sentence; not every base accepts every affix.

sections.label: Common Student Misconceptions
sections.final_normalized_text: Common Student Misconceptions3. Common Student MisconceptionsFeature spotting: Explain how the exact feature shapes meaning, communication or response.Retelling: Select precise evidence and analyse it rather than repeating content.Automatic effect: Interpret choices through audience, purpose, context and surrounding text.Vague explanation: Replace “this makes it better” with the exact feature, evidence and likely effect.A concrete quick correction“The story’s plot” means its connected events; “plot the heights” means mark the data. Quote a clue for the intended sense. An accurate sentence matters more than choosing the longest word.

Ask the student to show the exact clue, feature or language choice and explain or use it independently.A fresh vocabulary checkGiven record: a label is 7 centimetres long. Story: “At night in a tent, Bo lost a torch and found it in a bag.” Report the length, name the setting and a plot event, then explain bright in “The bright torch lit the tent” and “Bo had a bright idea”. Finally replace write again in “Bo will write the label again” with one related word.Check and explainThe label is 7 centimetres long. The setting is night in a tent. Losing or finding the torch is a plot event. Bright torch gives strong light; bright idea is clever or useful in this context. The surrounding words support the senses. Rewrite means write again: “Bo will rewrite the label.”
